items.item: Dijkstra's own correctness proof is exactly the claim that a vertex, once popped at its current-smallest distance, can never later be beaten — true only because every undiscovered extension of a path can only add a non-negative amount

items.item: The failure in the counterexample is not about the negative edge being on the shortest path to the wrongly-settled vertex — it is about the negative edge being reachable only through a vertex the algorithm has not yet settled when it settles the wrong one first

This topic's non-negative-weight restriction is the exact question the rest of the chapter answers by relaxing it: Bellman-Ford drops the restriction entirely by relaxing every edge repeatedly instead of settling vertices greedily

at.step: Dijkstra's algorithm settles the closest vertex first, and that greedy choice is only safe because no edge can ever make a path shorter by being added to it. The moment even one edge weight can be negative, that safety breaks, and the closest-first order stops being trustworthy.
